summary: A history of US payday lending from post-Civil War salary lenders and mob loan sharks to Scott Tucker's tribal-lending empire, industry-funded research and rolled-back federal rules, all profiting from trapping poor borrowers in debt.
keywords: Marquette National Bank v. First of Omaha

evidence.note: salary lending said to begin in the US in the late 1800s; chattel mortgage lenders after the Civil War
1978 Supreme Court ruling lets banks export home-state interest rates, birth of the modern industry
long Scott Tucker segment begins, originally planned as the whole episode
Charles Hallinan introduced as Tucker's mentor and later rival; both convicted around 2018
Tucker's lending run from Overland Park, Kansas, posing as tribal businesses
industry lawyer shaping academic studies to defend payday loans
2017 CFPB rules and their 2019 rollback under Trump bring the story to release
framing argument that delayed wages create the need for payday loans, revisited at length

notes: Primary subject is the industry/practice, so no roles. Mob loan sharking takes a real segment but there is no organized-crime theme. labor-exploitation rests on the hosts' extended argument about delayed pay. Hallinan birth year inferred from his age at sentencing; death status not verified. Tucker's racing career is brief, so sports omitted.
